cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: An AND gate outputs 1 only when ALL inputs are 1; its truth table has one high output for two inputs.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: An OR gate outputs 1 when ANY input is 1; it produces a low output only when all inputs are 0.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: A NOT gate (inverter) outputs the complement of its single input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: A NAND gate is the complement of AND: output is 0 only when all inputs are 1; it is a universal gate.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: A NOR gate is the complement of OR: output is 1 only when all inputs are 0; also a universal gate.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: An XOR (exclusive OR) gate outputs 1 when inputs are different; XNOR outputs 1 when inputs are the same.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: NAND and NOR are universal gates: any Boolean function can be implemented using only NAND or only NOR gates.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: Logic 1 typically corresponds to a high voltage (e.g. 5 V); logic 0 to a low voltage (e.g. 0 V).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: Truth tables list all possible input combinations and the corresponding output for each.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: For n inputs, a truth table has 2ⁿ rows covering every input combination.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: Logic gates are built from transistors; CMOS technology uses complementary pairs of MOSFETs.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Logic Gates
cards.back: Propagation delay is the time between a change at the input and the corresponding change at the output.
